atoms.text: Among the innovators of Soul music are singers like Aretha Franklin and Ray Charles, to name just two of many who began developing the genre in the 1950s. These core figures not only sang for entertainment, but to make their struggles heard and fight for their rights. In other words, they also used their voices for activism.

Known as the “Queen of Soul,” Aretha Franklin started singing in church as a child. Her music covered topics from love to pain to the struggle for equality. Her signature song, “Respect,” became an anthem for the Women’s Rights and Civil Rights movements. She once said: “We all require and want respect, man or woman, black or white. It’s our basic human right.” Her powerful voice and dazzling performances placed her among the greats, and she was the first woman to be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

Her powerful voice and dazzling performances placed her among the greats, and she was the first woman to be inducted into the Rock n' Roll Hall of Fame.

atoms.text: Ray Charles, another pioneer of Soul, was said to have begun playing piano at the age of five. He started to lose his sight soon after and went blind at the age of seven. Still, his lack of sight did not stop him from pursuing his love of music. He taught himself to play an array of instruments and particularly mastered the piano. By the time he was fifteen, he was touring the US and gained popularity across the country.

Like Franklin, Charles used music as a tool for social activism. His version of the song, “Georgia On My Mind,” described the segregation and racism he and other Black Americans experienced in the state and throughout the Jim Crow South. In 1961, he was scheduled to play a segregated show in Georgia, which was reserved for a white audience only. Charles refused to play the show, receiving a fine and risking his career. Such courageous acts and other forms of activism demonstrate that Charles was more than an entertainer; he was also an important supporter of the Civil Rights Movement.

Soul music stayed in style until the mid-1970s, when genres like Funk and Disco surpassed it in popularity. Nevertheless, Soul remains a significant style of Black American music with a lasting impression on US culture and history. Its defining characteristics, emotional presentation, profound lyrics and catchy beats continue to influence musicians worldwide.
